The first evening after Dadi's cremation, Madhuri did what she did best. At the kitchen table in their house in the kasba, she wrote out, in her neat engineering-notebook way, what had happened: the fall, the hip, the week in the district hospital, the pneumonia. Seeing it in order helped. Nothing felt random any more. Her friend Gurpreet called from college. "You sound very organised," Gurpreet said carefully.
"I am," Madhuri said. "But tomorrow at six, I'm going up to the terrace where Dadi dried her papads. No notebook. Just me."
The next evening she climbed up with Dadi's old shawl around her shoulders. She sat among the empty drying mats and let herself cry until the temple bell rang for aarti. Then she went down and helped her mother roll the rotis.

qa.q: Where did Madhuri go the next evening at six?
qa.a: Up to the terrace where Dadi dried her papads.

qa.q: Why did writing out the events help Madhuri at first?
qa.a: Seeing the fall, the hospital week and the pneumonia in order made the loss feel less random and easier to understand.

qa.q: Which choice kept Madhuri's notebook from becoming a hiding place?
qa.a: Deciding on a time and place to grieve without it, so understanding led her toward crying for Dadi instead of away from it.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet have felt hearing Madhuri sound 'very organised'?
qa.a: Gurpreet seemed a little worried the calm might be covering pain, and would likely be relieved to hear about the terrace plan.

grounding: A student uses her orderly, analytical habit to understand her grandmother's death and then deliberately makes time to grieve on the terrace.

Jamal studied statistics, so when his mum texted that Biscuit had died, he did what he knew. On the train back to his flat in Glasgow, he looked up the average lifespan of beagles, the early signs of kidney disease, the timeline the vet had described to his mum. By the time he reached the flat, he understood exactly why a fourteen-year-old dog stops eating. Nothing had been missed; nothing could have been done much sooner.
Bilal, his flatmate, found him at the kitchen table with a spreadsheet open. "Makes sense now," Jamal said. Then he closed the laptop. "I'm taking tonight off from understanding it."
He found the old video from the summer Biscuit learned to catch a ball on the bounce, and watched it three times. Bilal brought two mugs of tea and stayed. Around midnight, Jamal was laughing and crying at the same time.

qa.q: What did Jamal look up on the train?
qa.a: The average lifespan of beagles, the early signs of kidney disease, and the timeline the vet had described.

qa.q: What does Jamal's line 'Makes sense now' suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: Some relief that the death was understandable and not anyone's fault, along with a sense that understanding alone hadn't touched the sadness yet.

qa.q: What turning point shows Jamal using his analysis well?
qa.a: Closing the laptop and choosing to spend the night with the old video of Biscuit, so the understanding led into real grief instead of replacing it.

qa.q: What might the evening have been like for Bilal?
qa.a: Bilal watched a spreadsheet turn into laughter and tears, and by bringing tea and staying offered company without needing to fix anything.

grounding: A statistics student makes sense of his dog's death with research, then deliberately stops analysing and lets himself grieve with a flatmate nearby.

In her third week of clinical posting, Deepika's favourite patient on Ward 4, an old man who called her "doctor-ji" however often she corrected him, died in the night. The next afternoon, in the nursing college library, she read his chart notes twice and traced the fall in his oxygen levels against the sepsis chapter in her textbook. She could see where it had turned.
Her clinical instructor, Farida Ma'am, found her there. "Understanding it is good nursing," Farida said. "And the rest?"
Deepika hesitated. "After evening class I'll sit in the prayer room for half an hour. Just to miss him."
That evening she sat there with her notebook closed and cried quietly for the man who used to hum old film songs while she changed his dressings. Afterwards she felt tired, and lighter, and ready for the next shift.

qa.q: What did the old man on Ward 4 call Deepika?
qa.a: "Doctor-ji", however often she corrected him.

qa.q: Why did tracing the oxygen levels against the sepsis chapter feel useful to Deepika?
qa.a: It showed her where his illness turned, so the death made sense and she could learn from it as a nurse.

qa.q: Which choice helped Deepika's understanding lead toward her feelings?
qa.a: Setting aside half an hour in the prayer room with her notebook closed, so she could miss him instead of only studying his chart.

qa.q: How does Farida Ma'am seem to see Deepika's study in the library?
qa.a: She values it as good nursing but gently asks about 'the rest', showing she knows understanding a death is not the same as grieving it.

grounding: A nursing student studies a patient's decline to understand his death and then sets aside quiet time to grieve him.

Dear Ritu,
You asked how I'm coping since Shanta teacher died. Honestly, at first I did what I do in every lab: I made a timeline. When she first mentioned feeling tired, when she stopped coming to Sunday class, when her daughter called us. Writing it down helped. I understood it wasn't sudden, and that she had chosen to keep teaching as long as she could.
But I noticed I kept adding details and never once felt anything. So on Sunday I blocked an hour, five to six, like a class. I sat on the floor with her old harmonium book, the one with her pencil notes in the margins, and read them. By the third page I was crying properly, for the first time.
The timeline wasn't wasted. It told me what I was sad about. I think I needed both.
Write back soon,
Kalyani

qa.q: What did Kalyani sit with on Sunday?
qa.a: Shanta teacher's old harmonium book, the one with her pencil notes in the margins.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani decide to block an hour on Sunday?
qa.a: Kalyani felt uneasy that the timeline kept growing while no feeling came, and wanted the understanding to lead into the grief instead of standing in for it.

qa.q: Which choice turned Kalyani's analysis into a help rather than a wall?
qa.a: Setting a fixed time to actually feel the loss, with something personal like the pencil notes, so the timeline pointed toward the sadness instead of away from it.

qa.q: What might Ritu take from this letter?
qa.a: Ritu may feel relieved that Kalyani is not just coping on the surface, and might see a way of grieving that lets thinking and feeling work together.

grounding: Shows a student who first understands a teacher's death through a timeline and then sets aside time to feel it, so the understanding leads toward the grief.

You want to know how I've been since Bauji passed, Nirmala? Okay.
First week, I was all spreadsheet. Every doctor's visit, every report, the dates his medicines changed. I understood the illness better than anyone in the family. Chacha kept ringing me, "Gurpreet beta, what did the doctor mean?", like I was the expert. It felt good to be useful.
Then one night I caught myself reading about kidney function at two in the morning, and realised I hadn't once said I missed him. Not to anyone. Not even to myself.
So I made a rule. Every evening, after the reading, fifteen minutes with his old radio, tuned to the station he liked. No phone, no notes. First evening, nothing. Second, nothing. Third evening the old film songs came on and I just broke.
I think the reading was me walking toward it slowly. The radio was where I finally got there.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet turn on each evening?
qa.a: Bauji's old radio, tuned to the station he liked.

qa.q: What made Gurpreet realise the reading wasn't enough?
qa.a: Reading about kidney function at two in the morning without once saying "I missed him" showed Gurpreet the understanding had become a way around the grief.

qa.q: Why did the fifteen minutes with the radio work where the spreadsheet didn't?
qa.a: It paired the understanding with a set time to feel, using something tied to Bauji, so the sadness finally had a place to come out.

qa.q: How might things look for Chacha if Gurpreet had kept on playing the expert?
qa.a: Chacha would keep getting clear answers but might never see Gurpreet's grief, and the family could miss the chance to mourn Bauji together.

grounding: Illustrates a student who uses analysis to understand a grandfather's illness and then makes regular time to feel the loss, letting the thinking lead to the feeling.
